articles.title: How to run an issue panel

body.support:
An **issue panel** is a group of people with different views. They answer questions from an audience.

**1. Pick an issue.** Something people disagree about. It needs more than one side.

**2. The panel.** Three or four people, each with a different view. Each one gets ready:

- their view in one sentence
- two main points, with evidence
- a one-minute start.

**3. The host.** The **host** runs it. They give everyone a turn. They keep time. They ask: *“Can you give an example?”*

**4. The audience.** Everyone else writes questions. Good questions are:

- **short:** one question
- **open:** not just yes or no
- **fair:** about ideas, not people.

**5. Listen.** Take notes. What's each person's main point? Fact or opinion? Whose side are they on?

**6. Wrap up.** Write a short **summary**: the issue, the main points, and what you think.
body.core:
An **issue panel** brings people with different views together to answer questions from an audience. It's a great way to hear every side of an issue, and to make up your own mind.

**1. Pick the issue.** Choose something your class or community genuinely disagrees about: what to do with an empty block, a new rule, a local event, a transport change. It must have **more than one side**.

**2. Build the panel.** Choose three or four **panellists**, each with a different **perspective**: for example, a young person, a business owner, a parent and a council worker. Each panellist prepares:

- their **position** in one sentence
- two main points, with **evidence** (and they know which bits are facts and which are opinions)
- a short opening statement (one minute).

**3. Choose a host.** The **host** (or **moderator**) runs the panel. They introduce the issue and the rules, give everyone a fair turn, keep time, stop people talking over each other, and ask **follow-up questions**: *“Can you give an example?”* *“What's your evidence?”*

**4. Prepare the audience.** Everyone else writes questions on cards. Good questions are:

- **short**: one question, not three
- **open**: they can't be answered with just yes or no
- **fair**: about ideas, not attacking people.

*“How would this affect people who live nearby?”* is great. *“Why are you so selfish?”* is not.

**5. Listen actively.** While the panel talks, take notes. What is each person's **main argument**? Which parts are facts, and which are opinions? How does their **perspective** shape what they say? Is anyone leaving things out?

**6. Wrap it up.** At the end, the host sums up the main points. Then everyone writes a short **summary**: the issue, the main arguments, and your own view with evidence.
body.extend:
An **issue panel** brings together speakers with different positions to answer audience questions. It's a good way to explore an issue from several angles before you form a view.

**1. Choose an issue.** Pick a community issue people really disagree about, such as land use, a new rule, a local event or a transport change. It needs at least two fair positions.

**2. Build the panel.** Choose three or four **panellists** with different **perspectives**: for example, a young resident, a business owner, a parent and a council officer. Each one prepares a one-sentence **position**, two main points with **evidence** (and knows which parts are fact and which are opinion), and a one-minute opening.

**3. Appoint a moderator.** The **host** or **moderator** explains the issue and the rules. They give fair turns, manage time, stop interruptions, and ask **follow-up questions** that test evidence and reasoning.

**4. Prepare the audience.** Audience members write questions in advance. Good questions are short (one at a time), open, and about ideas rather than people.

**5. Listen critically.** Note each panellist's main argument. Separate facts from opinions. Think about how each speaker's perspective and interests shape what they claim, and watch for gaps that suggest bias.

**6. Pull it together.** The moderator sums up the main positions. Then everyone writes a **summary** of the arguments and their own view, backed by evidence.

caseStudies.title: Q+A: the audience asks

body.support:
**Q+A** is a show on **ABC TV**. It started in **2008**.

A panel of about **five** people sits in front of an audience. They have different views.

Then the **audience asks the questions**. People ask them live. Others send in videos.

A **host** runs it. The host gives everyone a turn. The host asks more questions when people dodge.

It isn't always calm. People disagree. But the audience gets to hear different sides.

Your class panel will work the same way.
body.core:
**Q+A** is a live discussion show on **ABC TV**. It first went to air on **22 May 2008**.

The idea is simple. A panel sits in front of a studio audience, usually **five** people with different views. Often there's someone from the government, someone from the opposition, and others like experts, writers or community leaders.

Then the **audience asks the questions**. People in the studio ask them live. Other Australians can send in video questions. The show's producers choose which questions get asked.

A **host** runs it all. **Tony Jones** hosted for more than ten years, until 2019. The host gives each panellist a turn, keeps time, and pushes them with follow-up questions when they dodge.

In **2010**, the show started showing viewers' tweets on screen, so people at home could join in. In **2020**, its name changed from Q&A to **Q+A**.

Q+A shows how a panel can bring different sides of an issue together in one room. It's not always calm. People disagree, interrupt and get frustrated. But the audience gets to ask what they want to know, and hear more than one answer.

Your class panel will be smaller. But it works the same way: different perspectives, a fair host, and the audience asking the questions.
body.extend:
**Q+A** is a live discussion program on **ABC TV**. It first aired on **22 May 2008**.

The format puts the audience at the centre. A panel, usually **five** people with different views, faces a studio audience. It often includes people from the government and the opposition, plus experts, writers or community figures. **Audience members ask the questions**, live in the studio or by sending in a video. Producers choose which questions go to the panel.

A **host** moderates. **Tony Jones** hosted for more than ten years, until 2019. He gave out turns, managed time, and pushed panellists with follow-up questions when they dodged.

The show has changed over time. From **2010**, it showed viewers' tweets on screen. In **2020**, its name changed from Q&A to **Q+A**.

Q+A shows both the value and the difficulty of a panel. Putting opposing views in one room lets the audience compare arguments directly. But discussion can get heated, so a good moderator is essential.

Your class panel uses the same structure, on a smaller scale: different perspectives, a fair moderator, and questions from the audience.

model.text:
**Issue:** Should our school have a four-day week?

**Arguments for**
- Students with jobs could work a full day without missing class.
- A longer weekend could help people rest.

**Arguments against**
- The other four days would be longer and more tiring.
- Some families need school open five days.

**The strongest point:** Mia said the longer days would be hard for students who catch the bus. I had not thought of that.

**My view:** I am against it for now. I would like a trial for one term first, to see what really happens.
why: It picks out the strongest point and says who made it.

teacher.overview: The Issues & Voices boss level. Students run a class issue panel on a community issue: they prepare roles (host, three or four panellists with different perspectives, and an audience with question cards), run a Q&A with openings, audience questions and follow-ups, then write a summary separating fact from opinion and stating their own view with evidence. The case study is ABC TV's Q+A, which since 22 May 2008 has put a panel with differing views in front of a studio audience that asks the questions.
prep: Choose (or let students vote on) a genuine local or school issue with at least two sides.
Prepare role cards for panellists with different perspectives.
Index cards for audience questions; a timer.
Optional: show a short, appropriate segment of Q+A to model the format.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** a one-sentence position, two points with evidence (fact or opinion), and a one-minute opening. Introduces the issue and rules, gives fair turns, keeps time, stops interruptions, asks follow-ups. Short, open, fair (about ideas, not people).

**Run sheet:** 1 host intro with rules; 2 panel with different perspectives; 3 timed openings; 4 audience questions chosen fairly; 5 follow-up for evidence; 6 close and summaries.

**Sort:** evidence question — good; selfish — fix; nearby residents — good; leading — fix; four-in-one — fix; other side gets right — good.

**Case study:** the audience asks what it actually wants to know; fair turns, time, follow-ups, calm; interruptions, attacks, one person dominating — use rules, timers and a firm host.
realityCheck: **Choose the issue carefully.** Local and concrete beats national and political.
**Role-play helps.** Students can argue a perspective they don't hold; make that clear.
**The host role is hard.** Coach a confident student, or co-host yourself.
**Keep it respectful.** Set rules up front and enforce them kindly.
**Works in a real class:** yes. A lively finish to the zone.
